arXiv:2611.20316

Authors: Boyang Chen, Claire E. Heaney, Christopher C. Pain

Submitted: Nov 2026 | Updated: Nov 2026

This paper presents a method for solving the shallow water equations on highly distorted structured grids using convolution-based operators following the Neural Physics approach. By mapping distorted physical grids to a uniform computational domain with Jacobian transformations, the governing advection and diffusion operators are reformulated in a structured convolutional form. This enables the use of efficient stencil-based operations and, following the Neural Physics concept, we do this through convolutional layers whose weights are determined by the chosen numerical methods rather than by training. The method introduces consistent mass-lumped formulations, conservative and non-conservative advection forms, and a diffusion operator, all expressed as convolutions. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

##### Summary

Underwater image enhancement (UIE) research is trending toward heavy models, while lightweight alternatives are judged by parameters and FLOPs: proxies that say little about latency and energy on the edge accelerators underwater IoT platforms deploy. We report an on-device measurement study of shallow-water enhancement, whose per-channel attenuation physics favors compact quantized networks. Depthwise-separable U-Nets (9k-59k parameters) and a 4.3k-parameter curve model are trained on UIEB, quantized to FP16, INT8, and INT4 (palettized) with weight-only post-training quantization, and deployed via Core ML on the CPU, GPU, and Apple Neural Engine (ANE) of an Apple M3 Pro, with per-frame energy from idle-subtracted SoC power counters. The main 28.9k-parameter model at INT8 on the ANE enhances 256 × 256 frames at 945 FPS and 4.7 mJ/frame with no degradation at the reported two-decimal precision relative to FP16, and +3.2 dB PSNR over raw input on a 90-image held-out UIEB split. Across all 36 configurations on this FP16-compute stack, weight-only quantization provides no consistent latency or energy gain; energy is governed by compute-unit choice (3.6× vs. the GPU, 5.5-5.6× vs. the CPU) and network width. A W8A8 variant engages the ANE integer datapath (-18% latency, -28% energy at -0.37 dB), localizing the neutrality to weight-only PTQ rather than to the model or the NPU. A sub-30k-parameter network already saturates the measured quality-cost trade-off.

Developing quantum algorithms to simulate fluid dynamics has become an active area of research, as accelerating fluid simulations could have significant impact in both industry and fundamental science. While many approaches have been proposed for simulating fluid dynamics on quantum computers, it is largely unclear whether these algorithms will provide speedup over existing classical approaches. In this paper we give evidence that quantum computers cannot significantly outperform classical simulations of fluid dynamics in general. We continue our study on the convergence issue of the intermediate long wave equation (ILW) on both the real line and the circle. In particular, we establish convergence of the scaled ILW dynamics to that of the Korteweg-de Vries equation (KdV) in the shallow-water limit at the $L^2$-level. Together with the recent work by the first three authors and D. Pilod (2024) on the deep-water convergence in $L^2$, this work completes the well-posedness and convergence study of ILW on both geometries within the $L^2$-framework. Our proof equally applies to both geometries and is based on the following two ingredients: the complete integrability of ILW and the normal form method. More precisely, by making use of the Lax pair structure and the perturbation determinant for ILW, recently introduced by Harrop-Griffths, Killip, and Vişan (2025), we first establish weakly uniform (in small depth parameters) equicontinuity in $L^2$ of solutions to the scaled ILW, providing a control on the high frequency part of solutions. Then, we treat the low frequency part by implementing a perturbative argument based on an infinite iteration of normal form reductions for KdV.

Solving inverse and optimisation problems with traditional shallow water equations (SWE) solvers can be computationally expensive, particularly when gradients with respect to model inputs or parameters must be estimated through repeated forward simulations. In this paper, we introduce DiffSWE2d, an open-source differentiable shallow water equations solver for end-to-end flood and tsunami modelling implemented in PyTorch. By leveraging automatic differentiation, DiffSWE2d represents the time-marching physics as a differentiable computational graph, enabling gradients to be propagated directly through the numerical solver. We validate the solver against two established benchmark cases and demonstrate its application to tsunami waveform inversion, showing its ability to infer model inputs through gradient-based optimisation. DiffSWE2d provides a flexible framework for integrating physics-based hydrodynamic modelling with modern optimisation and machine learning methods. The source code and reproducible examples are publicly available at: https://github.com/ZhonghouXu/DiffSWE2d
